↳ Posted by laura nesbit on March 14th, 2002.

Roche Collection

The title “Frank Roche’s” was attached when this tune was published in the Roche’s Collection, which was edited by (you guessed it) Frank Roche. It is, as weescottishfiddler notes above, a setting of William Marshall’s “Lady Ann Hope” but (sorry mairtin) strathspeys and flings really are different! In Ireland, flings imported from Scotland were played for two-hand social dancing and occasionally the figure of a set. The Scottish fling is a solo dance in competitions, I believe. The strathspey is still a solo dance in Cape Breton, as it once was in Scotland. To turn a strathspey into a fling, you generally have to simplify it a bit and play it with the right rhythmic pulse, which is approximately “get OFF me, get OFF me,” etc.

↳ Posted by blarneystar on October 26th, 2006.

This tune was actually composed by John Pringle, first appearing in 1800 in a collection of Pringle’s own tunes.

↳ Posted by niall_kenny on October 27th, 2007.

Why notated in common time?

I recently got into Irish tunes, and “studied” some of Molloy’s tunes on “stony steps”.
Before I looked up the sheetmusic on here, I notated the tune in 12/8. Because listening to this tune, I don’t hear it in Common Time (metre 2/2) as Molloy plays all quavers uneven ( they would sound odd considering all the triplets in this tune).

Another thing which puzzles me: Molloy performs the triplets like triplets, not like it is often done: 2 semiquavers + 1 quaver.

Hence my 2 questions:
1. is there a difference in the execution of triplets between Irish and Scottish music
2. is it common practice to change 2 quavers into one crotchet and one quaver, in a tune with lots of triplets? (thus giving the tune a “swinging” character).

↳ Posted by Bart De Mylle on October 19th, 2008.

A strathspey will never be transcribed in 12/8. I don’t know exactly why: a Scottish dancer would know. But, anyway, why do you bother notating the tune or looking at the sheet music? Just trust your ears.

↳ Posted by slainte on October 19th, 2008.

…triplets …

Bart, if you listen carefully, you’ll find that those triplets of Molloy’s on this tune (same for other players too) are *not* even. To a classical listener, I guess they would sound ‘rushed’. Yet, somehow, they never force the beat ahead of itself, as it were. But seriously, they’re not even. They’re really not like a classical player would play the three, evenly spaced in the time of two quavers.

Also, the long-short rhythm of this, and other flings and strathspeys is *not* the same rhythm as a crotchet and two quavers in 12/8 time. Listen to Molloy - they vary quite a bit, and quite often they will be more like a dotted quaver/semiquaver, to use classical terminology.

As slainte implies, you have to listen to get it.

↳ Posted by ethical blend on October 19th, 2008.

I thought bout notating it in 12/8, because of the long-short rhythm of this, but I realize that they vary quite often.

It’s common practice in this sort of tune to play the ‘long-short’ type of rhythm. But I wouldn’t describe it as a crotchet followed by a quaver. Which, I think, is why they’re not generally notated that way.

Re: Frank Roche’s

“Is there a difference in the execution of triplets between Irish and Scottish music?”

In Scottish fiddle music I know not, but in Highland piping the triplets in Strathspeys is one of those things that varies from player to player. You can have three top pipers using three different approaches to timing them. It’s not “anything goes” but rather a range of timing approaches that are deemed proper.

The timing varies from “tight” to “open”.

The mathematically proper “two sixteenth-notes and one eighth-note” is more even, more “open”, than even the most-open triplets you would hear, I think. They would never be played as actual triplets, that is, three even notes in the space of two.

On a music-writing program I once wrote out a Strathspey just to see how one would have to write the timing to get the computer to play back the tune sounding proper, with the “lift” a Strathspey is supposed to have. It was a complicated thing to do, all the strange note-values I had to use.

BTW calling a Scottish tune with a known composer and title by the title of the Irish collection it happened to appear in makes no sense- if it did we would have over a thousand Irish tunes that everyone would call “Francis O’Neill’s”.

Re: Frank Roche’s

Some people have said that this tune, Frank Roche’s Favourite, is a version of the Scottish tune, Lady Anne Hope. And some Scottish members have said it’s an inferior version.

In this regard, I’ve noticed that there seems to be an element of chauvinism on the part of some Scottish self-styled music connoisseurs on the question of Scottish music versus Irish music. They seem to be misconstruing “different” as “inferior”. But that’s another day’s work.

I can discern little or no resemblance between Lady Anne Hope and Frank Roche’s Favourite; and, for what it’s worth, the latter is a far nicer tune to my ears. In fact, it’s been one of my favourite tunes to play for decades, and I have no desire whatsoever to learn the Scottish “version”.

Which, by the way, is not to say that there are not many gorgeous Scottish tunes. I have a great fondness for both of these great musical traditions.

Re: Frank Roche’s

A bit of clarification is required here, as not everyone has done their homework. I’m looking at a copy of “The Athole Collection”, right in front of me. There are TWO tunes, both strathspeys, with the same title “Lady Ann Hope”. The strathspey on page 111 is unquestionably the original source of the tune which has entered the Irish tradition and was recorded by Matt Molloy as “Frank Roche’s Favourite”. The second strathspey is also titled “Lady Ann Hope” with "( No. 2 ) to the right of the title, and bears little resemblance to the tune recorded by Matt Molloy, which is the one being discussed here.
Hope this helps.

Re: Frank Roche’s

Hi John, again! Let’s clear the air.

1) If you’ve heard any Scottish people saying that our music is superior, I’m sorry. I have never come across that way of thinking in several decades of being involved in traditional music.

2) While DonaldK might have been a little harsh in his criticism of The Chieftains video above, I’m sure it was an opinion about a particular performance, and not in any way a statement of general superiority/inferiority.

3) For your information, Jimmy Shand (1908-2000) recorded that set in 1945, some 42 years before Matt Molloy’s recording. The Scots fiddler George F Davie recorded it in 1934 under the title “The Jimp Waist.” The dancer/fiddler John “Dancie” Reid recorded it in 1931, as did Donald Davidson, the great harmonica player. Fiddler Robert Kirk recorded it in 1930, and A J Scott recorded a melodeon setting in 1911.

4) We are all incredibly lucky that we love traditional music in all its forms, variations, settings. “Frank Roche’s Favourite” is a great tune. I also like “Miss Ann Hope/Lady Ann Hope.”

5) Peace, brother.

In my previous searches I had not come across that video by Paul Anderson, though I had seen at least one other video by him. That’s a lovely rendition of both those tunes – Scottish music at its best.

His rendition of the Lady Ann Hope strathspey is very different from the version titled Frank Roche’s Favourite played by Irish musicians such as Matt Molloy and even the version by the Waterboys.

I think I can understand now why Donald K was so dismissive of the Chieftains’ version. It’s easy to see that if one were Scottish and therefore familiar and attuned to the original Scottish version, which is really gorgeous, one could view the “Irish” version as almost sacrilegious.

Since I had never heard the original Scottish version, I responded to the intrinsic beauty of the tune itself even in spite of its “Hibernification”.

Slán go fóill.

Re: Frank Roche’s

I think I see what you mean, Donald. As the Chieftains became more famous and commercially successful a certain “drawing room” vibe seemed to creep into their music - especially when the harp came into it. I still think they were brilliant in their earlier output, which of course was very much influenced by the great Seán O Riada.

That flute version of the tune that you posted naturally reminds me of Matt Molloy’s version which, not surprisingly, is the “Irish” version that I like best. It doesn’t have the Scottish “snap” but makes up for it by Molloy’s typically dynamic energy and fluidity, which Seamus Heaney likened to a squirrel let loose in a church.
